name: Prasat Ta Krabey
significance: A small laterite Khmer sanctuary on the Dangrek escarpment, raised under Suryavarman I and Udayadityavarman II and left unfinished, enclosing a linga called Svayambhuva. It stands on the contested Cambodia-Thailand frontier and its carvings include Yama riding his buffalo mount.

name: Wat Kamphaeng Laeng
significance: A walled Khmer complex of four laterite towers and a cruciform shrine built in the reign of Jayavarman VII, the westernmost surviving Khmer sanctuary in Thailand. An image of Uma recovered here in 1956 marks its Hindu foundation; the site later became a Buddhist wat.

name: Gopinath Temple, Pabna
significance: A Vaishnava brick temple in Pabna town built by Brajmohan Krori, a tahsildar under the Nawabs of Murshidabad, in the jor-bangla form of two joined do-chala roofs. Its terracotta panels illustrate Ramayana and Mahabharata scenes; the image was moved to a nearby Kali temple in 1910 and worship has ceased.

name: Shadani Darbar
significance: A Hindu shrine in Mirpur Mathelo taluka founded in 1786 by Sant Shadaram Sahib, reported to be the largest Hindu temple in Sindh. Its liturgy combines agni puja with recitation of the Bhagavad Gita and the Guru Granth Sahib, and the saint's birth anniversary draws an annual gathering.

name: Saraswati Gyan Mandir
significance: A temple to Saraswati on the University of Chittagong campus, financed by Adul Kanti Chowdhury and Anita Chowdhury through their foundation; its foundation stone was laid in 2019 and it opened in 2026. It gives the university a permanent shrine for the Saraswati Puja long observed there, and is described as the only one of its kind in Bangladesh.

name: Phra That Narai Cheng Weng
place: That Na Weng, Mueang Sakon Nakhon
significance: A sandstone Khmer prang on a laterite base outside Sakon Nakhon town, carved with a lintel showing Krishna slaying a lion in Baphuon-period style. It is the principal Khmer Hindu monument surviving in the province.
story: Local tradition holds that the sanctuary was raised entirely by women, in a building contest against the men who put up Phra That Phu Pek.

name: Prasat Huai Thap Than
significance: A Khmer sanctuary of the Baphuon period whose three towers on a shared platform stood for the Trimurti, registered as a national monument in 1935. Rebuilt under Lan Xang influence in the 18th-19th centuries, it passed into Buddhist use and its name changed from Prasat Ban Prasat to That Chedi and then to its present form.

name: Mahilara Sarkar Math
significance: A brick math at Mahilara in Gournadi raised by the local notable Sarkar Rup Ram Das Gupta under Nawab Alivardi Khan, built for Shiva and painted inside with Radha-Krishna imagery. Its tiered octagonal spire, with cornice mouldings that borrow from European church design, now leans noticeably and is the only tilted temple of its kind in Bangladesh.

name: Prasat Kao Noi
style: Khmer, late Sambor Prei Kuk to early Prei Kmeng
significance: Three east-facing brick towers on a shared base near Aranyaprathet, put up in the 7th century under Isanavarman I or Bhavavarman II and reckoned the oldest Khmer monument of consequence in Thailand. Lingas and pedestals found here had been broken into fragments, evidence that the shrine was deliberately desecrated.

name: Sindurmati Tirthadham
deity: Durga, Krishna, Vishnu, Rama and Kali
significance: A pilgrimage site around a large tank on the Kurigram-Lalmonirhat boundary, founded by the zamindar Raj Narayan Chakraborty and carrying shrines to Durga, Krishna, Vishnu, Rama and Kali. The complex was restored under a government programme in 1975.
story: A childless zamindar is said to have dug the tank in hope of offspring and named his two daughters Sindur and Moti after they were born; during a Navami puja held at the centre of the tank the water rose and drowned them, and after he dreamed that they had become immortal the water took their names.

name: Bhairabkunda Shiva Mandir
significance: A Shiva shrine in southern Bhutan near the Assam border, first built in timber after the 1950 Assam-Tibet earthquake and replaced by the present structure between 2002 and 2005. Its design deliberately blends Hindu temple forms with traditional Bhutanese architecture, and it draws pilgrims from across the frontier.
story: It is counted among the Shakta pithas where a part of Sati fell; Indra is said to have meditated here on his celestial elephant, Bhairab Nath to have found a self-formed Shiva lingam at the spot, and a cave beneath the temple to mark where Shiva himself meditated.

name: Prasat Phanom Wan
significance: A Khmer sanctuary outside Khorat, founded in the 11th century for Maheshwara and rebuilt in sandstone in the 13th-14th centuries, with a main prang of three arched gateways joined to a surrounding cloister. It later passed into Buddhist use and was listed as an ancient monument by the Fine Arts Department in 1936.

name: Kalka Cave Temple
significance: A cave shrine to Kali at Aror near Sukkur, known as the Asthan of Kalka Devi and one of the few active Hindu pilgrimage places in upper Sindh. Devotees gather there on the evening of the first Monday of each month.
story: Kalka Devi is said to have manifested at this spot while travelling to the Hinglaj Mata temple, and the shrine's caretaker holds that two tunnels in the cave run all the way to Hinglaj.

name: Burmese Buddhist Temple
significance: Singapore's Theravada temple in the Burmese tradition, begun in 1875 by U Thar Hnin and rehoused on Tai Gin Road in 1991; it is described as the only Burmese temple outside Myanmar built in the traditional Burmese manner, with teak carving throughout. Its 3-metre image, carved in 1918 from Sagyin marble and shipped 2,500 km to Singapore in 1921, is the largest pure white marble Buddha outside Myanmar.

name: Manuha Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (three seated images and a reclining parinirvana image)
significance: A two-storey rectangular shrine at Myinkaba in Bagan, finished in 1067 by Manuha, the captive Mon king of Thaton. Its four colossal images - three seated Buddhas and one entering final nibbana - are wedged so tightly into their chambers that the cramped setting is read as an expression of the king's captivity.
story: The Glass Palace Chronicle relates that Manuha, in remorse, raised the great images and prayed that wherever he might be reborn in samsara he would never again be conquered by another.

name: Ramkot Banashram
deity: Gautama Buddha (chest-bone relic; image in abhaya mudra)
significance: A hilltop monastery near Ramu, held to be one of the stupas raised in Ashoka's reign and named from words meaning chest bone, for the relic of the Buddha it is said to enshrine. Lost for centuries, it was rediscovered after a stone inscription came to light and was restored in 1919 by the Sri Lankan monk Jagat Jyoti Mahasthavir.
story: Tradition holds that the Buddha came here with Ananda and foretold that a pagoda would one day stand on the spot to hold a relic from his chest.

name: Taung Mingyi Pagoda
significance: One of the four great pagodas of Amarapura, built in 1786 by the minister Thaung Mingyi and sheltering a standing Buddha image nearly 14.3 metres high. Wrecked by the earthquake of 1838, it was rebuilt on the order of King Pagan Min from 1850 and finished under Mindon in 1853; the 2025 Myanmar earthquake damaged it again.

name: Kothduwa Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (Bodhi tree grown from the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi)
significance: An island temple in the Madu Ganga estuary reached only by boat, built in the 1860s by the businessman Samson Rajapakse around a Bodhi tree raised from the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi. It is remembered as a resting place of the Buddha's tooth relic in the fourth century.
story: Princess Hemamali and Prince Danthakumara are said to have carried the tooth relic from India disguised as brahmins, the relic hidden in the princess's hair, and to have concealed it at Kothduwa before handing it to King Sirimeghavanna.

name: Sri Lankaramaya Buddhist Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (brass image presented by Jawaharlal Nehru)
significance: A Theravada temple begun in 1920 by the Singapore Sinhala Buddhist Association; Sir Franklin Gimson laid the foundation stone of the present building in 1949 and it opened in 1952. It holds a brass Buddha given by Jawaharlal Nehru and a Bodhi tree descended, by way of the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, from the tree at Bodh Gaya.

name: Aluvihare Rock Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (reclining, standing and seated images)
significance: A cave monastery north of Matale, traced to the reign of Devanampiyatissa, whose caves carry painted walls and ceilings, Buddha images and early inscriptions. It is remembered above all as the place where the Pali Canon was first committed to writing under King Walagamba in the 1st century BCE; the site was declared a protected monument in 1974.

name: Tu Dam Temple
significance: A Hue monastery founded in the late 17th century by the Lam Te Zen master Thich Minh Hoang and granted the title Sac Tu An Ton Tu by the Nguyen lord Nguyen Phuc Chu in 1703; Emperor Thieu Tri renamed it Tu Dam in 1841. A bodhi offshoot from Bodh Gaya was planted in its forecourt in 1939.

name: Tamote Shinpin Shwegugyi Temple
deity: Gautama Buddha (three encased images and a reclining Buddha)
builtDisplay: 11th c. core, encased in a stupa in the 14th c.
style: Cave temple within an encasing stupa
significance: A temple near Kyaukse begun as a single-storey hall under Anawrahta, given a second storey by Narapatisithu, then wholly enclosed in a stupa by Uzana I of Pinya in the 14th century, so that a pagoda hides a pagoda which in turn hides a two-storey temple. Its upper terrace carries stone-carved Jataka reliefs, and it was gazetted as an ancient heritage site in 2015.

name: On Lang Assembly Hall (Quan Am Temple)
significance: A Hokkien assembly hall and temple in Cho Lon, raised by Fujianese immigrants in the late 19th century and centred on Quan Am, the bodhisattva of mercy. Pure Land worship of Amitabha sits alongside altars to the sea goddess Mazu and the Jade Emperor, and its statuary includes tableaux from Journey to the West.
